questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The theory that can completely/properly explain the nature of bonding in $\left[Ni{\left(CO\right)$}_{4}\right]$ is:$
questions.solution:
There is synergic bonding present in $\left[Ni{\left(CO\right)}_{4}\right]$.

As $CO$ is neutral ligand, so oxidation state of nickel is zero i.e.${Ni}^{0}$.

So, electronic configuration of ${Ni}^{0}$= \left[Ar\right]3{d}^{8}4{s}^{2}$

As $CO$ is strong field ligand, it will back paired the 4s electrons to $3d$ orbitals.

So in complex electronic configuration of ${Ni}^{0}$= \left[Ar\right]3{d}^{10}4{s}^{0}$ here inner d orbital is filled.

In ligand $CO$ (carbonyl) the anti-bonding orbital is vacant.

$CO: \sigma1{s}^{2}, \sigma * 1{s}^{2}, \sigma2{s}^{2}, \sigma * 2{s}^{2}, \sigma2{p}_{z}^{2}, {\pi p}_{x}^{2} = {\pi p}_{y}^{2}, \pi * {p}_{x}^{0} = \pi * {p}_{y}^{0}$

The fully filled inner d-orbital of central metal atom gives it's electrons to vacant $\pi$ anti-bonding orbital, this is called back $\pi$ bonding, due to this back bonding bond between metal and ligand is very strong.

This back $\pi$ bonding is also called synergic bonding and this synergic bonding is explained by molecular orbital theory.

Carbon monoxide $CO$ made synergic bonding with Haemoglobin in are blood, as synergic bonding is very strong, so oxygen taking capacity of haemoglobin decrease and it cause death.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Complete removal of both the axial ligands (along the $z - axis$ ) from an octahedral complex leads to which of the following splitting patterns? (relative orbital energies not on scale).
questions.solution:
When crystal field splitting energy is small, the pairing energy exceeds the splitting energy, and the electrons will fill the d orbitals as if they were degenerate; this is classified as high spin.

We find that the square planar complexes have the greatest crystal field splitting energy compared to all the other complexes. This means that most square planar complexes are low spin, strong field ligands.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A reaction of cobalt $( III )$ chloride and ethylenediamine in a $1: 2$ mole ratio generates two isomeric products $A$ (violet-coloured) and $B$ (green-coloured). $A$ can show optical activity, but, $B$ is optically inactive. What type of isomers do $A$ and $B$ represent?
questions.solution:
The coordination number of cobalt is $6$.

The mole ratio of ${CoCl}_{3}$ and $en$ is $1: 2$.

Hence,

${CoCl}_{3} + 2en \to \left[Co{\left(en\right)}_{2}{Cl}_{2}\right]Cl$

The complex formed shows geometrical isomerism.

The complex exists as cis and trans isomers among which the trans isomer is optically inactive.

questions.q: Homoleptic octahedral complexes of a metal ion $′{M}^{3 +}′$ with three monodentate ligands ${L}_{1}, {L}_{2}and{L}_{3}$ absorb wavelengths in the region of green, blue and red respectively. The increasing order of the ligand strength is:
questions.solution:
Observed order of wavelengths, ${\lambda}_{abs}$= {L}_{3} > {L}_{1} > {L}_{2}$.

(Red light has highest wavelength of 700 nm while blue is the shortest with a wavelength of about 480 nm)

So, ${∆}_{0}$ (strength of ligands) order will be ${L}_{2} > {L}_{1} > {L}_{3}$.

(As ${∆}_{0}\alpha\dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{abs}}$ )

Hence, order will be ${L}_{2} > {L}_{1} > {L}_{3}$.

Therefore, Strength of ligand $∝ {∆}_{Absorption}$.

questions.q: The total number of possible isomers for squareplanar $\left[\mathrm{Pt}(\mathrm{Cl})\left(\mathrm{NO}_2\right)\left(\mathrm{NO}_3\right)(\mathrm{SCN})\right]^{2-}$ is:
questions.solution:
The square planar complex of the type $[\mathrm{Mabcd}]^{\mathrm{n} \pm}$, where all four ligands are different, has 3 geometrical isomers. But if one of the ligands is ambidentate, then $2 \times$3=6$ geometrical isomers are possible. But if two ligands are ambidentate, then $4 \times 3=$ 12 geometrical isomers are possible.
In the given example, $\mathrm{NO}_2^{-}$and $\mathrm{SCN}^{-}$are ambidentate ligands.

questions.q: Which of the following complex ions has electrons that are symmetrically filled in both ${t}_{2g}$ and ${e}_{g}$ orbitals?
questions.solution:
Metal ion having either ${d}^{5}\text{or}{d}^{10}$ configuration can be filled symmetrically in both ${t}_{2g}\text{and}{e}_{g}$ orbitals. ${Co}^{+ 2}$ has ${d}^{7}$ configuration, ${Co}^{+ 3}$ has ${d}^{6}$ configuration. ${Mn}^{+ 2}$ has ${d}^{5}$ configuration but ${CN}^{-}$ is strong field ligand and it will pair the electrons due to which electronic configuration is ${{t}_{2g}}^{5}{{e}_{g}}^{0}$.

As $F$ is weak field ligand hence back pairing of electrons do not take place or in case of weak field ligand pairing energy of electrons (P )is greater than crystal field splitting energy in octahedral complex $\left({∆}_{o}\right)$ i.e.$P > {∆}_{o}$ , hence electrons will go in ${e}_{g}$ orbitals, instead of back paired in ${t}_{2g}$ orbitals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: One mole of the complex compound $\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5 \mathrm{Cl}_3$, gives 3 moles of ions on dissolution in water. One mole of the same complex reacts with two moles of $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$ solution to yield two moles of $\mathrm{AgCl}$ (s). The structure of the complex is
questions.solution: $\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5 \mathrm{Cl}_3\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5 \mathrm{Cl}\right]^{+2}+2 \mathrm{Cl}^{-} \therefore$ Structure is $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5 \mathrm{Cl}\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2$.
